title: Ukraine: Perils for Kyiv in revived peace talks
gist: Revived US-brokered Ukraine peace diplomacy (Oslo, St Petersburg, a possible Trump-Putin-Xi meeting at APEC Shenzhen) looks like progress but the author argues terms favour Moscow, which still seeks Donbas, a compliant Kyiv and neutrality.

insights.claim: US envoy Stephen Witkoff met Zelenskyy and European representatives in Oslo on 20 October, then Putin in St Petersburg on 21 October, with Russia agreeing in principle to resume technical three-way talks with Ukraine and the US, possibly in mid-November.
insights.speaker: Ian Hill
insights.so_what: Watch mid-November talks for any concrete settlement terms.
insights.locator: US special envoy Stephen Witkoff met

insights.claim: Russia called the European and Ukrainian ideas conveyed by Witkoff 'not very useful' and says the key is building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the war, leaving unclear what territorial concessions Kyiv would face.
insights.speaker: Ian Hill
insights.so_what: Ambiguity on territory is the core risk to Ukraine in any framework.
insights.locator: Witkoff went on to St Petersburg

insights.claim: Putin has proposed a trilateral meeting with Trump and Xi at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, and Trump has responded positively, though he would prefer a denuclearisation agenda.
insights.speaker: Ian Hill
insights.so_what: A Yalta-style summit could produce understandings on Ukraine made over Kyiv's head; watch the APEC agenda.

insights.claim: China is unlikely to agree to nuclear arms control talks while its fast-expanding arsenal remains inferior to those of Russia and the US, so a denuclearisation focus is hard to sustain.
insights.speaker: Ian Hill
insights.so_what: Lowers odds that an APEC trilateral yields arms-control progress.
insights.locator: It is hard to see Beijing agreeing

insights.claim: A Shenzhen summit would likely produce at most an understanding on key elements of a settlement rather than a full deal, and the author sees Ukraine faring poorly in any outcome.
insights.speaker: Ian Hill
insights.so_what: Risk skewed toward terms favourable to Moscow.
insights.quote: Whatever the outcome, it’s hard to see Ukraine coming out well out of it.

insights.claim: Putin will not accept a deal short of Russia's core objectives: control of all of Donbas, a compliant government in Kyiv, and Ukrainian neutrality, while Russian aerial bombing aims to strengthen its negotiating position.
insights.speaker: Ian Hill
insights.so_what: Expect no real Russian de-escalation absent these terms; sustained strikes on Ukraine infrastructure continue.

insights.claim: Zelenskyy has offered to freeze current front lines for a ceasefire, but Kyiv needs bankable US and European security guarantees before any long-term deal.
insights.speaker: Ian Hill
insights.so_what: Security-guarantee substance is the key signal to track.

insights.claim: The US has leverage over Ukraine, shown by an apparent brief curtailment of US intelligence support and denial of Starlink access, and could restrict European-funded US weapons supplies.
insights.speaker: Ian Hill
insights.so_what: Washington pressure on Kyiv is a live lever for forcing a deal.
insights.locator: If the US were to throw its weight

insights.claim: Zelenskyy has recently resisted US pressure by resuming attacks on Russian refineries and oil infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Ian Hill
insights.so_what: Continued strikes on Russian energy infrastructure are relevant to oil product supply.
insights.locator: For Kyiv the war is an existential struggle

insights.claim: European support for Ukraine is secure for now but the outlook is more uncertain, as key centrist European governments face elections next year under pressure from populist parties unsympathetic to Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Ian Hill
insights.so_what: European political risk in 2027 could erode Ukraine funding.
insights.locator: For Kyiv, continuing European support is crucial
